summary: Compiles clarifications to the original iSCSI definition in RFC 3720 as a companion document for implementers. It updates RFC 3720 and overrides it where they differ. It was replaced by RFC 7143.

eli5.summary: A list of fixes and clearer wording for the iSCSI rulebook. A newer RFC replaced it.

subtitle: Clarifications and fixes to the iSCSI protocol for implementers.

tldr.problem: The original iSCSI protocol in RFC 3720 left some implementation details ambiguous, and fielded implementations revealed issues that needed clarification.
tldr.mechanism: This document compiles explicit clarifications, corrections, and new semantics for iSCSI behavior, covering data residual handling, multi-task abort operations, discovery session semantics, and error recovery.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have clearer guidance on non-obvious protocol aspects, improving interoperability. The document was superseded by RFC 7143.

today: RFC 5048 has been superseded by RFC 7143, which consolidates iSCSI protocol specifications. Implementers should refer to RFC 7143 for current iSCSI protocol details.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 3720 defines the iSCSI protocol, which carries SCSI commands and data over TCP/IP. Since its publication, many iSCSI implementations have been built, and that real-world experience revealed ambiguities and issues in the original specification. This document serves as a companion guide for iSCSI implementers, offering critical guidance on non-obvious implementation aspects and clarifying points where the original text was unclear or incorrect.

The document does not rewrite RFC 3720 but instead updates and supersedes specific sections where there is conflict. Implementers must reference RFC 3720, RFC 3722 (string profiles) and RFC 3723 (security) alongside this document.
sections.eli5: Building the actual systems that use iSCSI taught people where the rules were fuzzy. This explains the fuzzy parts more clearly so everyone can build systems that work together.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
Several key concepts anchor the clarifications. SCSI-Presented Data Transfer Length (SPDTL) is the total data the SCSI layer hands to iSCSI for a task. Expected Data Transfer Length (EDTL) is what iSCSI expects based on the command header. When they differ, the task has a residual — overflow if SPDTL exceeds EDTL, or underflow if it is less.

For multi-task operations, the document defines affected tasks — the set of tasks impacted by a task management function such as abort or reset. For a logical unit reset, for example, all outstanding tasks from all initiators on that LU are affected.

The document also introduces the TaskReporting negotiation key, which allows sessions to opt into two modes: standard RFC 3720 behavior or the faster FastAbort semantics designed to improve error recovery.
sections.eli5: When data doesn't match expectations, iSCSI signals whether too much or too little arrived. Task management needs to know which tasks are affected by an abort or reset command.

sections.title: Data Residual Handling and Overflow Rules
sections.content:
Section 3.1 clarifies how iSCSI reports mismatches between expected and actual data. When SPDTL exceeds EDTL (overflow), the target must set the overflow flag and report the residual count as SPDTL minus EDTL. When SPDTL is less than EDTL (underflow), the underflow flag is set and the residual is EDTL minus SPDTL.

A detailed example clarifies the SCSI REPORT LUNS command, which has an allocation length field that may be smaller than the full LUN list. If the target SCSI layer truncates data to fit, and iSCSI's EDTL accommodates that truncated amount, no overflow occurs — even though more data existed at the SCSI level. This prevents false overflow signals when the protocol is working correctly.

The document also updates rules on R2T ordering: multiple Ready-To-Transfer PDUs must be fulfilled in order within a single task, but no ordering relationship exists between tasks on a connection.
sections.eli5: When the target has more data than the command asked for, or less, iSCSI flags it and says how much difference there is. For list commands that truncate intentionally, the protocol correctly recognizes no overflow happened.

sections.title: Task Management and Abort Semantics
sections.content:
RFC 5048 clarifies and extends task management behavior. It defines a base set of clarified multi-task abort semantics that all implementations must follow. When an ABORT TASK SET, CLEAR TASK SET, or reset is issued, both initiators and targets follow a precise sequence: waiting for outstanding data transfers and responses, propagating the task management request to the SCSI layer, and ensuring no responses are delivered after a task management response that would imply the tasks are still active.

Additionally, the document defines FastAbort semantics, an optional faster recovery mode. Instead of waiting for all outstanding transfers to complete, FastAbort allows the target to send asynchronous messages telling the initiator to stop sending data, then free resources later after the initiator acknowledges. This speeds up error recovery on multi-connection sessions.

The document introduces the response fence concept: certain SCSI responses (like the first response after a multi-task abort) must be strictly ordered with respect to earlier responses on the same logical unit, even on multi-connection sessions. This ensures the initiator sees status in a consistent order.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong and many tasks need to stop, iSCSI has a careful dance: tell everyone to stop, wait for confirmations, then release resources. A faster way lets the target interrupt faster and clean up later.

sections.title: Discovery Sessions, Error Handling and PDU Semantics
sections.content:
Discovery sessions — used to query targets without logging in fully — follow special rules. The document clarifies that error recovery level must always be 0 for discovery sessions. For session reinstatement, it distinguishes between unnamed discovery sessions (those without a target name) and named discovery sessions. Unnamed sessions use a simplified reinstatement rule based on the portal address, not the target name.

Section 7 addresses error handling edge cases. An ITT (Initiator Task Tag) value of 0xffffffff is reserved and only appears in target-initiated NOP-In messages. The document clarifies what constitutes a format error (such as a NOP-In with a valid target transfer tag but an invalid LUN). For digest errors on unsolicited PDUs like Async or Reject messages, the entire PDU including its header must be discarded and treated as a lost response, not silently ignored.

Finally, Section 8 introduces a new asynchronous event code 5 for task termination (used with FastAbort) and deprecates Reject reason code 0x0b, which has no legitimate protocol use case.
sections.eli5: Discovery sessions are quick lookups and have simpler rules. When errors occur, the protocol must be clear about what to discard and what to retry. New event codes signal when tasks are being dropped.
